children: By Erin Mulvaney and Cara Lombardo
As Weil, Gotshal & Manges edges toward a merger with a rival, more top lawyers are heading for the exits, intensifying pressure on the beleaguered law firm to secure its future.
Among the people leaving are two members of Weil's management committee, appellate lawyer Drew Tulumelo and securities litigation partner Caroline Zalka, according to people familiar with the matter.

Tulumelo is expected to join Davis Polk, along with another litigation partner, Chantale Fiebig, the people said. Zalka is headed for Paul Weiss. Lyuba Goltser, co-managing partner of the firm's corporate department, will join Sidley Austin.
The expected departures add to a string of others by some of Weil's leaders in the past year, most notably its top dealmaker, Michael Aiello.
Law.com earlier reported on Zalka's departure.

The exits this year have intensified questions about Weil's future, but its woes predate that. The elite restructuring and private-equity powerhouse with some $2.1 billion in revenue has seen stagnant growth in recent years relative to its top rivals. The firm has said it remains healthy and is adding new lawyers and clients.

This week, Weil told partners it was in merger talks but didn't name the suitor, according to people familiar with the matter. Only a small group knows the name of the other firm, which couldn't be learned.
The talks are with another U.S. firm and a potential tie-up would likely create a firm that would rank in the top 10 by revenue, one of the people said. Weil currently ranks in the top 30.
There are no guarantees a deal will come together.

Top law firms have been racing to remake themselves in recent years as talent wars and the threat of artificial intelligence upend their business models. The rise of mega firms, such as Kirkland & Ellis and Latham & Watkins, are making it harder for even elite firms such as Weil to compete.
Similarly sized firms to Weil, including Willkie Farr & Gallagher, have shown interest in finding merger partners in recent years, according to a person familiar with the matter.

Over the past year Weil has been quietly reaching out to rival law firms, including Vinson & Elkins, about potential mergers, people familiar with those discussions say. Some firms have approached Weil as well. Many of those talks, including those with Vinson & Elkins, didn't progress.
Merger talks accelerated after the news that Aiello was departing for Cravath, Swaine & Moore.

Competitor firms have recently received an influx of résumés from Weil's lawyers. Other exits have included London dealmaker David Avery-Gee and Michael Hickey for Sullivan & Cromwell. London finance head Tom Richards plans to go to Simpson Thacher.

Weil Gotshal, founded in 1931, was a pioneer among elite firms in building a restructuring practice, leading some of the largest bankruptcies in history, including Lehman Brothers, General Motors, Enron, and WorldCom.

The boon from the financial crisis solidified its reputation as a restructuring force. But it was slower than some peers to reinvest in expanding its business and cut lawyers when the bankruptcy work dried up, according to legal industry observers.

Amid the current turmoil, Weil has been undergoing a leadership transition. Earlier this year, it appointed private-equity partner Ramona Nee to replace Barry Wolf, who has served as the firm's leader for 16 years.
